# The deterministic checker: what it catches, and where it stops

**Task owner:** Maia — Week 3. Generated by `checker_boundary.py`; do not hand-edit. Offline, no API key, reproducible in seconds.

`checker.py` recomputes every stated derived value from its own components and asserts systolic > diastolic. No model, no prompt, 387 lines. It is the upper bound on how much of this corpus needs no language model at all — and stating that bound honestly is the point of this document.

**Across all 676 built conditions, 232 of which are contradictions: the checker catches 95/232.**

## What it catches

| family | condition | catch rate | if silent, why |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | contradiction | 35/35 (100.0% [90.1% - 100.0%]) | — |
| B | contradiction | 60/60 (100.0% [94.0% - 100.0%]) | — |
| C | contradiction | 0/30 (0.0% [0.0% - 11.4%]) | structural: a criterion asserted and then denied leaves no numeric trace; no arithmetic exists to run |
| breadth | contradiction | 0/67 (0.0% [0.0% - 5.4%]) | implementation: two values for one input ("chloride 101 and 80.8"); label-anchored patterns read the first or neither |
| dissociation | value_conflict | 0/40 (0.0% [0.0% - 8.8%]) | implementation: two values for one input ("creatinine 1.4 and 0.5"); label-anchored patterns read the first or neither |

Families A and B are caught completely: 100% on both, and the clause's "near-perfect" turns out to be exactly perfect. Every other contradiction in the corpus is missed.

## The boundary — and why it is two boundaries, not one

The temptation is to report one number: *the checker misses 137/232 contradictions, so those need a model.* That would overstate our own limit in the direction that flatters the paper. Two different things are happening.

**30 items are structurally invisible.** Family C asserts a criterion and later denies it — "history of diabetes … no history of diabetes". There is no number in disagreement with another number. No version of this tool, however good, could ever catch these. This is a real boundary and it is where a language model is genuinely required.

**107 items are missed for an implementation reason.** The dissociation and breadth arms inject two values for one input: `chloride 101 and 80.8 mEq/L`, `creatinine 1.4 and 0.5 mg/dL`. `checker.py` reads quantities with label-anchored patterns, so the second value falls outside the match — and in the breadth arm the conflicted quantity is not read at all, not even recorded as ambiguous. A duplicate-value detector would catch all 107 of these. How long that would take is a guess, not a measurement -- but the change is local to `read()`, and nothing else in the tool would have to move.

Measured directly — on duplicate-value contradiction items, how often the checker failed to read the conflicted quantity at all:

| family | conflicted quantity | is it a quantity the checker tracks at all? | not read, of the contradiction items |
|---|---|---|---|
| breadth | the conflicted input | yes, all of them — but the phrasing defeats the pattern | 67 |
| dissociation | creatinine | no — no formula here consumes it, so it never looks | 40 |

**So the honest claim is narrower than "the checker cannot reach these."** What we can say is: arithmetic alone already solves Families A and B; a modestly better arithmetic tool would also solve the dissociation and breadth arms; and Family C is the only part of this corpus where a language model is not merely convenient but necessary. Family C is 30 items.

## The cost side

**False positives on clean notes: 0/202 (0.0% [0.0% - 1.9%]).** The checker never fires on a note that is not broken. That matters, because a check that flags healthy notes is not a free upper bound — it is a cost. This one is free.

**But it fires on 65/202 (32.2% [26.1% - 38.9%]) resolvable notes** — and that is a limitation worth stating before someone else does. A resolvable item is the contradictory note plus a cue *in the question* naming which value governs. The checker never sees the question. So a pipeline that gated on this checker would refuse notes that are perfectly answerable, and every A and B resolvable item is one of them.

| family | checker fires on resolvable |
|---|---|
| A | 35/35 (100.0% [90.1% - 100.0%]) |
| B | 30/30 (100.0% [88.6% - 100.0%]) |
| C | 0/30 (0.0% [0.0% - 11.4%]) |
| breadth | 0/67 (0.0% [0.0% - 5.4%]) |
| dissociation | 0/40 (0.0% [0.0% - 8.8%]) |

## Known gaps this does not close

- `docs/CHECKER_INPUT_EXTRACTION_GAP.md` — the height/weight blind spot, which bounds the Family A number from below.
- Duplicate-value detection, discussed above. Not implemented, deliberately unclaimed.
- The checker reads notes only. Anything stated in the question is outside its view, which is what the resolvable row above measures.

## Reproduce

```
python3 checker_boundary.py
```

No API key, no cache, no model. Every number above comes from `checker.py` run over `data/items_*.json`.
